discipline_framing: Perceptual psychology applied to data visualization — how the brain automatically groups shapes, identifies patterns, and recognizes anomalies, and how designers engineer those automatic processes deliberately
audience: Data visualization designers, dashboard and BI developers, information designers, and front-end engineers who must make graphics that the visual system parses instantly and correctly — without conscious effort from the viewer
sources: Wertheimer, Koffka, and Kohler's classical Gestalt psychology (laws of perceptual organization, Pragnanz) as the founding tradition
Palmer, Rock, and Ehrenstein's modern re-analysis of gestalt principles (the new gestalt grouping factors: convexity, symmetry, parallelism, common-region research)
Ware, Information Visualization: Perception for Design — the applied-perception canon bridging vision science and interface design
Treisman's feature-integration theory and the visual-search literature (pop-out, conjunction search, anomaly detection)
Cleveland and McGill's graphical-perception experiments (the elementary-task accuracy hierarchy) as the quantitative complement to grouping theory
Tufte's information-design doctrine (data-ink, chartjunk, small multiples) read through perceptual-grouping lenses
Nielsen Norman Group and applied-UX research on proximity, similarity, and common-region effects in interface layouts
pitfalls: Teaching the laws as a memorized list (proximity, similarity, closure) without the underlying perceptual-organization problem they solve, producing decoration-by-checklist instead of engineered perception
Ignoring accidental grouping — unintended alignments, adjacency, and shared styling creating false patterns and phantom relationships viewers cannot unsee
Over-grouping dense dashboards into cards and boxes until the containers carry more ink and attention than the data
Confusing grouping salience with importance — strong gestalt structure on the wrong element directing attention away from the decision-relevant signal
Assuming universality — grouping strengths vary with expertise, culture, and task; what pops for the designer who knows the answer may not pop for a first-time viewer
